text.tspan: Both frames below are the same picture. On the left is what gets copied: a face, a headline, a logo, a pose, each of which belongs to somebody. On the right is
the same picture written as a brief: where the light is, how much of the frame the subject takes, what is left empty, and what order it reads in. Everything on
the right is free. Nothing on the left is. The table underneath gives each axis a verdict, so the answer to "can I use this" is a row rather than a feeling.

svg.text: What a beginner takes. Four boxes, four owners.
What a brief takes. Same frame, none of the ownership.
Eleven axes, with a verdict on each

text.tspan: Take it as it is
What is this image trying to do: make
known, prove, sell, or retain?
The job itself. Nobody owns 'this is a proof
image'.
Nothing. This is the one axis with no
rights risk at all.

svg.text: Cái giữ mắt ở giây đầu

text.tspan: Take the idea, change the
thing
In the first second, what holds the eye?
That a hook exists, and roughly where it sits
in the frame.
The device itself. A splash, a torn
edge, a hand entering frame — reuse it
and you have made the second-best
version of somebody else's picture.
Take it as it is
What is understood first, second, and
third?
The order, as three numbered positions.
Write it down as 1, 2, 3.
The exact type sizes and the exact
words that carried it.
Take it as it is
Where does the subject sit, and where is
the empty area for type?
Crop ratio, subject position, the rectangle left
empty, the horizon height.
A distinctive layout device: a signature
diagonal split, a recognisable grid
gimmick.
Take the idea, change the
thing
What stands at the centre: product,
person, mechanism, or place?
The category of subject, and how much of
the frame it fills.
The specific person, the specific
product, the specific place.
Take it as it is
Where does the light come from, hard or
soft, and is the camera high or low?
Source direction, height, size, hardness,
colour, camera height and distance.
Nothing, as long as you describe it
rather than name the photographer.
Take the idea, change the
thing
What are the surfaces: glass, paper, skin,
metal, fabric, food?
How the material behaves under that light —
where it goes glossy, where it stays matte.
The same material set. Changing
material is one of the three axes you
must move.
Take the idea, change the
thing
What does the type do: claim, prove, or
call to action?
The rhythm and the density: how many
words, in how many blocks, doing which
job.
The words. Every single one of them.
Take the idea, change the
thing
If it moves: what changes state, and over
how long?
The pacing, and the count of state changes.
The exact shot order. A copied
sequence is recognised faster than a
copied frame.
Note it, then do not use it
How many times has this category
already done this?
The finding. A saturated device is a useful
thing to know and a useless thing to use.
The device. That is the entire point of
scoring this axis.
Do not put it in a prompt at
all
Is there a real person's face, a logo, a
character, or a named artist's signature?
Nothing from this axis enters a prompt.
Record it and stop.
Everything: the face, the logo, the
character, the style-of-a-named-artist.
Three axes say transform, and reference-analysis.md asks you to move at least three before using a pattern at all. That is not a coincidence: hook, material and copy behaviour are
the three that carry the most recognition, so moving them is what stops a reference being traceable at a glance. If the result can still be traced to one source, start again.
